to Aleppo,
and he seized Rashid al-Din, who had fled there,
and brought him and imprisoned him in the fortress called Habij.
From it, none of those who were imprisoned in it had ever escaped death at all,
except for this one, who was later shown mercy and saved.
For in the wall of this fortress,
over a very high precipice,
there was a door,
and outside of it, a certain small plank,
on which a man could barely manage to stand, without being able to sit.
And when a sentence of death was issued against someone from among the honored nobles,
and they did not wish to lay hands on him and kill him,
they would bring him out
and make him stand on that plank,
and shut the door in his face.
And after he stood for a day or two,
he would be overcome by sleep, fall off, and die.
All these things, and the going to and fro to the Tatars, took place within three years.
And in the year one thousand
five hundred and sixty of the Greeks [1249 AD], when that Baha al-Din arrived, and Tatars with him,
the vizier Shams al-Din al-Isfahani was afraid,
and he wished to take Sultan 'Izz al-Din
and go in and rebel in one of the maritime fortresses.
And there was in Iconium one of the nobles, an old servant of Sultan 'Ala al-Din,
whose name was Jalal al-Din Qaratay,
an ascetic man who abstained from eating meat and drinking wine, and from women,
good and merciful.
This man, when he perceived that the vizier was about to take 'Izz al-Din and flee,
sent and seized him in his house,
and cast him into irons,
and quickly made it known to Baha al-Din.
And he sent Tatars,
and they came and tortured this Shams al-Din al-Isfahani,
until he confessed {OCR?} and showed them endless treasures;
and then they killed him.
This man was a scholar who was very skilled,
and when he perceived that they were going to put him to death,
he composed elegies for himself in Persian,
mournful words, full of sorrow, yet very polished and sweet.
And when this man was killed,
Jalal al-Din became the regent of Sultan 'Izz al-Din,
and the countries were divided between the two brothers.
